newsitem.title: ESTONIA: INTERVIEW-ESTONIA BOURSE HEAD SEES 10-20 LISTINGS '97.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-ESTONIA BOURSE HEAD SEES 10-20 LISTINGS '97.

text.p: Between 10 and 20 new companies will be listed on the Tallinn Stock Exchange this year, the exchange's managing director Helo Meigas said on Wednesday.
Currently there are only eight listed companies in Estonia.

In an interview in her office, Meigas also told Reuters that the number of members on the exchange would increase this year from the current 24, with negotiations with four new members nearly completed.
"The number of shareholders will increase this year... with negotiations ongoing wth four companies to join as members," Meigas said.
She said the first of these new members would probably join in the summer, after the exchange celebrates its first anniversary in May.
Meigas said she did not want to release more details of the new members yet. All of them are Estonian.
"There has been some foreign resident companies that have inquired about the possibility of becoming a member but so far there has been no concrete steps taken," she said.
Meigas said the number of companies wanting to list on the exchange was also growing rapidly.
"Optimistically up to 20 more companies could be listed this year but more realistically I see the number at around 10," she said.

"This will give investors a lot more choice. Our main problem from the foreign investors' point of view is that we are so small. This increase may help us to attract foreign investors into the market."

The exchange at the end of last year had a market capitalisation of US$800 million and investment in 1996 came 60 percent from Estonians. the market capitalisation has increased to US$900 million this year.
No new companies have been listed on the exchange so far this year as the exchange needs first of all to see their audited results for 1996 and these are only just starting to come in.
She said she expected the first listing to be in late April or early May.
Meigas said at least half of the eight companies now on the free market would probably be listed this year.
"Companies consider it to be much more prestigious to be on the main list," Meigas said.
Currently companies on the free market are not obliged to disclose any information about themselves.
Companies on the secondary market and main list are subject to the same disclosure rules.

The difference is that a company on the main list has to have a market capitalisation of at least 100 million kroons and three years of audited results whereas a company on the secondary list needs a market capitalisation of 10 million kroons and two years of audited results.
"But we are a little worried that maybe some companies are starting to like being on the free market too much," Meigas said.
"The board is to make a final decision later this month about whether to impose any requirements on the free market or whether to proceed with the free market at all."
Meigas said the new listings were not expected to significantly lift the market capitalisation.
She said it was only when infrastructure companies like Estonia Gas or Estonian Telecom listed on the exchange, possibly next year, that the market capitalisation would alter significantly.
